clue.text: Statement made by one Swedish misogynist

definitions.text: Statement made by one Swedish misogynist

parts.note: surface reading: a famous line spoken by a Swedish person, which points to the film star Greta Garbo
setter's reading: a woman-hater would wish to be without any female company at all

explanation.surface: Someone quotes a remark made by a Swedish man who dislikes women.
explanation.walkthrough: Greta Garbo, the Swedish film actress, is famous for the line 'I want to be alone'; read as 'a lone', it is also what a misogynist wants: no women around.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is Garbo's celebrated quotation, and a hater of women would equally wish for solitude from them.

clue.text: Translation of meaning

definitions.meaning: first sense: rendering spoken words into another language
second sense: the sense someone reads into something

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase about translating meaning, but it is two separate senses joined by 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: An interpreter's work is oral translation, and an interpretation of a text is also its understood sense or reading.

clue.text: Girl able to turn up a whole lot of dates

parts.note: a girl's name

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something up makes it read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to be able is to be capable of doing

explanation.surface: A girl manages to show up with an enormous number of dates for her.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests romantic dates; the definition means calendar dates.
explanation.definitionFit: An almanac is an annual calendar listing days, festivals, tides and other events by date.

clue.text: With Henry gone, sells their material for lattice screens

indicators.note: the letters are treated as raw material to be fashioned into something new
gone means taken away, so the henry abbreviation is dropped from the following words

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
taken as written

explanation.surface: After Henry leaves, a shop sells its fabric intended for screens.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove H from SELLS THEIR and rearrange the nine letters that are left.
explanation.definitionFit: Trellises are frameworks of crossed strips, used as garden screens or plant supports.

clue.text: Instruments provided when Ian and Oscar play together

indicators.note: the two names mingle in play, their letters mixed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two friends, Ian and Oscar, make music together on some instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocarinas are small egg-shaped wind instruments with finger holes, a kind of musical instrument.

clue.text: A dramatic group outing?

parts.note: surface reading: an exciting trip taken by a party of people
setter's reading: the theatrical direction telling several actors to walk off stage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dramatic' means of the theatre, and 'outing' is going out: the Latin stage direction for several characters leaving together.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin stage direction means 'they go out', marking the departure of more than one actor.

clue.text: Nothing right for boyfriend

parts.note: love is a score of nothing in tennis
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone decides that having no partner is the right choice over a boyfriend.
explanation.definitionFit: A lover is a romantic partner, so a boyfriend is one example.

clue.text: A prospective candidate?

parts.note: surface reading: a person who might one day stand for office
setter's reading: someone formally put forward, named for a post or award

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a vague description of a hopeful; it simply describes someone proposed for election.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who has been put forward is a would-be winner, standing for selection or election.

clue.text: Horses that are for the high jump

definitions.text: Horses that are for the high jump

parts.note: surface reading: an idiom for being in serious trouble and about to be punished
setter's reading: animals that race over tall fences and water jumps

explanation.walkthrough: 'For the high jump' is British slang for facing punishment; here it means literally bound for big jumps in a race over fences.
explanation.definitionFit: These racehorses compete in a race over high hurdles and ditches, named after old church-tower to church-tower races.

clue.text: Mild? Or consumed by rage?

parts.note: a temper is a fit of rage
ate means consumed; 'consumed by rage' is read as rage, then consumed

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person is calm or eaten up with anger.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers two opposite states; the second is wordplay giving a fit of rage followed by a word for eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: Temperate weather or behaviour is moderate, free of extremes, so mild is a synonym.

clue.text: Very old with German propensity to throw up

parts.note: V is the abbreviation for very
O is the abbreviation for old
mit is the German word for with

explanation.surface: An ancient person with a German tendency to be sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Propensity to' adds nothing to the letters; it only makes the surface read smoothly into the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To vomit is to be sick, bringing food back up, the same as throwing up.

clue.text: Children always have some of the kidneys

indicators.note: having only some means the letters are taken from part of the words that follow

parts.note: letters running across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Kids always eat a portion of the kidneys at mealtime.
explanation.definitionFit: Renal is the medical adjective relating to the kidneys, as in renal failure.

clue.text: Another one racing around, showing lack of knowledge

indicators.note: asks for a different version of the words that follow, a new arrangement of them
the letters are moved around, spun into a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A second runner dashes about, revealing that it has no idea where it is going.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignorance is the state of not knowing, a want of information or education.

clue.text: Was rich, perhaps, having hidden a thousand in a wheelchair?

indicators.note: something hidden is tucked away inside, so one piece goes within the other
suggests the words are only one possible version, so their letters can be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
K is short for a thousand, as in 10K

explanation.surface: A formerly wealthy person stashed a thousand pounds in a wheelchair.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as playful: a pulled cart is a chair on wheels.
explanation.definitionFit: A rickshaw is a light two-wheeled passenger cart, humorously a chair with wheels pulled by a runner.

clue.text: Have it for breakfast before driving through American state

indicators.note: something driving through another passes into its middle, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: Cal is an abbreviation for California
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: Someone eats breakfast before setting off on a drive across an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole phrase: 'it' is the thing you have for breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: Cereal, such as cornflakes or porridge, is the standard morning meal eaten from a bowl.

clue.text: English parents stumble round to find a common language

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: stumbling throws things into disorder, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: English parents fumble their way about trying to find a shared tongue abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like a container signal; here it is the letter shaped like a circle, added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto is an artificial language invented in 1887 to be a universal second tongue for all.

clue.text: Charlie made certain to be told off

parts.note: Charlie is the radio code word for C
to ensure is to make certain

explanation.surface: A man called Charlie made sure he would get a scolding.
explanation.definitionFit: To censure is to criticise formally, so censured means reprimanded or scolded.

clue.text: Office worker gets somehow t-tipsy

indicators.note: somehow implies the letters get there in some unspecified way, rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the stammered letter included

explanation.surface: A clerk somehow ends up slurring drunkenly after an office party.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter in 't-tipsy' is not just colour: the extra letter is needed for the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A typist is a clerical employee whose job is typing documents, classic office staff.

clue.text: Terrible panic about the Spanish bird

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes around the other
something terrible is in a bad state, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A frightful panic breaks out concerning a bird from Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: The pelican is a large water bird with a long beak and throat pouch for catching fish.

clue.text: Like a tyrant, coped with its development

indicators.note: development turns material into a new form, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A country dealt with its growth under an oppressive ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is an absolute ruler, so despotic means behaving tyrannically.

clue.text: Norse god taking opium? Work abandoned on radioactive metal

parts.note: Thor is the Norse god of thunder

indicators.note: abandoned means left behind, so the work abbreviation is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: A god of Norse myth on drugs downs tools to work on a radioactive element.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorium is a naturally radioactive chemical element, a metal used as a nuclear fuel.

clue.text: Purchased a bit of wood? One ton

parts.note: a bough is a branch, a bit of a tree
T is the abbreviation for a ton

explanation.surface: Someone bought a chunk of timber that weighs a whole ton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wood' suggests timber but a bough is part of a tree in a wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Bought is the past tense of buy, so it is a direct synonym for purchased.

clue.text: Programmes on the box with seemingly endless appeal

definitions.text: Programmes on the box with seemingly endless appeal

parts.note: surface reading: television shows that are enduringly popular
setter's reading: very long broadcasts that are fund-raising appeals

explanation.walkthrough: 'Appeal' sounds like charm or popularity; it means a request for donations, and the shows run for hours. 'The box' is British slang for television.
explanation.definitionFit: These are lengthy television broadcasts raising money for charity, so a long-running plea for donations.

clue.text: Short extract from Chapter Seven

indicators.note: an extract is a passage taken from inside a longer text, so the letters lie within

parts.note: letters spanning the end of one word and start of the next

explanation.surface: A brief passage lifted from the seventh chapter of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Terse means brief and curt, using few words, so short is a synonym.

clue.text: In fresh air little woman goes back to the wine

indicators.note: placed in signals one piece goes inside the other
going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters are read right to left

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: fresh means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

parts.note: Jo is a woman's name, and Little Women is the novel in which she appears

explanation.surface: Out in the open air, a small woman returns to her glass of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Jo March is the heroine of Louisa May Alcott's Little Women, hence 'little woman'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rioja is a Spanish red wine from the region of the same name, so it is a wine.

clue.text: Happen to have small volume in our grasp

indicators.note: something held in a grasp is enclosed within a hand, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
cc is short for cubic centimetre, a small volume

explanation.surface: We happen to hold a little book in our hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small volume' suggests a little book; it is the measurement abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To occur is to take place or come about, a direct synonym for happen.

clue.text: Given rude version of verbal noun

definitions.note: strictly a gerundive is a Latin verbal adjective; the gerund is the verbal noun

indicators.note: a version is a different rendering, so the letters are given a new form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grammar student is handed a vulgar rendering of a part of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Grammarians would call a gerundive a verbal adjective, so the definition is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: A gerundive is a Latin grammatical form derived from a verb, closely related to the gerund.

clue.text: Marks given for quotations about butterflies that have turned up?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the punctuation that encloses quoted speech
second meaning, whimsical: the comma is a butterfly, and turned up means upside down

explanation.walkthrough: The comma is a species of butterfly named for the white comma-shaped mark on its wing; 'turned up' means flipped over, not arrived.
explanation.definitionFit: Quotation marks look like upside-down punctuation commas, and the comma is also a butterfly species.
